title: Sorting algorithms
description:
Implement sorting yourself (no `Arrays.sort`, `Collections.sort` or `List.sort`):

```java
class Sorts {
    static void insertionSort(int[] a)                       // in place
    static int[] mergeSort(int[] a)                          // returns a new sorted array; a is unchanged
    static long countInversions(int[] a)                     // pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j], in O(n log n)
    static <T> void stableSort(List<T> list, Comparator<? super T> cmp)   // a stable merge sort of the list, in place
}
```

`countInversions` measures how far an array is from sorted: `{2, 4, 1, 3, 5}` has 3 (2>1, 4>1, 4>3). Count them while merge sorting: when an item from the right half is taken before the remaining items of the left half, it forms an inversion with each of them. The tests use 100 000 numbers, too many for an O(n²) count.
hints: Write one private recursive method that sorts a range **and** returns the number of inversions in it; `mergeSort` and `countInversions` can both use it on a copy.
Stability comes from taking the left item when the two are equal (`<= 0`), so equal items keep their order.
